title: AI Datasets
answer: Training and evaluation datasets with size, licence, provenance, language coverage, and documented bias.

reading.body:
AI datasets are catalogued in three groups, and licensing and provenance is the largest of them, with 17 entries against 9 evaluation sets and 8 training corpora.

The split is the useful signal. The smallest group is the training data itself, the corpora that actually feed pre-training. The largest is the legal and provenance layer that governs whether those corpora may be used at all. For AI specifically, this suggests the constraint on data is being felt less as a shortage of text and more as a question of rights, and the catalogue reflects that by tracking permission and origin more heavily than raw volume.

The three groups also cover different things. Training datasets are recorded with provenance and licence. Evaluation datasets are recorded by what each benchmark actually measures, which is a check on whether a score means what it claims. Licensing and provenance covers what may lawfully be used for what, and how to tell.

What this does not contain is any dataset itself. There are no sizes, no language counts, no bias findings, and no named corpora in the data, only the structure of the catalogue and the number of entries in each branch. It says nothing about compute, buildings, or power, and no link between dataset supply and the grid can be drawn from it.
